claim: In Bfl-1:FS2, position 3c is positioned closer to helix 2 of Bfl-1 than in Bfl-1:PUMA.
source: In Bfl-1:FS2, position 3c is positioned closer to helix 2 of Bfl-1 than in Bfl-1:PUMA, allowing R3c to fill the space left by an adjacent methionine-to-alanine mutation at 3d when it adopts this hydrogen-bonded position.

claim: R3c fills the space left by an adjacent methionine-to-alanine mutation at 3d when it adopts the hydrogen-bonded position with N51.
source: In Bfl-1:FS2, position 3c is positioned closer to helix 2 of Bfl-1 than in Bfl-1:PUMA, allowing R3c to fill the space left by an adjacent methionine-to-alanine mutation at 3d when it adopts this hydrogen-bonded position.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: N51 at this position of helix two is unique to Bfl-1 among the human anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: N51 at this position of helix two is unique to Bfl-1 among the human anti-apoptotic proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Modeling FS2 mutations in the Bfl-1:PUMA structure suggested that the small-to-large mutation of alanine at position 2a in PUMA to valine in FS2 would result in steric clashes with helix 4 of Bfl-1 for all backbone-dependent rotamers.
source: Modeling FS2 mutations in the Bfl-1:PUMA structure suggested that the small-to-large mutation of alanine at position 2a in PUMA to the valine in FS2 would result in steric clashes with helix 4 of Bfl-1 for all backbone-dependent rotamers (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The shift in the Bfl-1:FS2 structure accommodates the valine at position 2a.
source: This change is accommodated by the shift in the Bfl-1:FS2 structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: A rotation of FS2 in the Bfl-1 binding groove partially buries the phenylalanine at position 1g that is solvent-exposed in the PUMA complex.
source: Also, a rotation of FS2 in the Bfl-1 binding groove partially buries the phenylalanine at position 1g that is solvent-exposed in the PUMA complex, which may be energetically favorable (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Partial burial of the phenylalanine at position 1g may be energetically favorable.
source: Also, a rotation of FS2 in the Bfl-1 binding groove partially buries the phenylalanine at position 1g that is solvent-exposed in the PUMA complex, which may be energetically favorable (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural analysis.

claim: The designed Bfl-1 library was re-scored on the shifted Bfl-1:FS2 structure using STATIUM.
source: Because the altered binding mode of FS2 is expected to impact predictions made using structure-based models, we re-scored the designed Bfl-1 library on the shifted Bfl-1:FS2 structure using STATIUM.
evidence: This is a description of the computational analysis methods.

claim: FS1 and FS2 scored much better on the shifted model than on the original model.
source: FS1 and FS2 scored much better (higher) on the shifted model than on the original model, whereas PUMA scored better on the original model (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis, shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PUMA scored better on the original model than on the shifted model.
source: FS1 and FS2 scored much better (higher) on the shifted model than on the original model, whereas PUMA scored better on the original model (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis, shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sequences that passed screening were enriched in sequences that scored better on the shifted model, compared to the input library.
source: Analysis of the entire pool of sequences that passed screening showed that these peptides were enriched in sequences that scored better on the shifted model, compared to the input library, consistent with our observation of size patterning in the majority of these sequences (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis, shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of FS2 bound to Mcl-1 was solved at 2.35 Å resolution.
source: To better understand the structural basis of FS2-binding specificity, we solved the X-ray crystal structure of FS2 bound to Mcl-1 at 2.35 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the structural biology methods and results.

claim: FS2 binding to Mcl-1 is >100 fold weaker than binding to Bfl-1.
source: FS2 binding to Mcl-1 is >100 fold weaker than binding to Bfl-1.
evidence: This is a finding from the binding assays.

claim: FS2 engages Mcl-1 in a shifted orientation relative to BIM.
source: Similar to the way FS2 binds to Bfl-1, FS2 engages Mcl-1 in a shifted orientation relative to BIM (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The shift in FS2 binding to Mcl-1 re-positions the aspartate at peptide position 3f to a location 4.8 Å away from Mcl-1.
source: As is the case for FS2 binding to Bfl-1, this shift re-positions the highly conserved aspartate at peptide position 3f to a location 4.8 Å away from Mcl-1, disrupting the canonical salt bridge with arginine 92 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The shift in FS2 binding to Mcl-1 disrupts the canonical salt bridge between D3f and arginine 92.
source: As is the case for FS2 binding to Bfl-1, this shift re-positions the highly conserved aspartate at peptide position 3f to a location 4.8 Å away from Mcl-1, disrupting the canonical salt bridge with arginine 92 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Disruption of the D3f:R92 salt bridge doesn't account for the specificity of FS2 for Bfl-1, because the salt bridge is lost in both Bfl-1:FS2 and Mcl-1:FS2 complexes.
source: This disruption would be expected to reduce affinity for Mcl-1, but it doesn't account for the specificity of FS2 for Bfl-1, because the salt bridge is lost in both complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: R3c in FS2 forms a hydrogen bond with N51 of Bfl-1.
source: For example, R3c in FS2 forms a hydrogen bond with N51 of Bfl-1, but does not form an equivalent interaction with Mcl-1 and is instead solvent exposed (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: R3c in FS2 does not form an equivalent interaction with Mcl-1 and is instead solvent exposed.
source: For example, R3c in FS2 forms a hydrogen bond with N51 of Bfl-1, but does not form an equivalent interaction with Mcl-1 and is instead solvent exposed (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In Mcl-1, there is an alanine (A55) at the site corresponding to N51 in Bfl-1.
source: In Mcl-1, there is an alanine (A55) at this site, and an adjacent histidine (H53) would be expected to clash with R3c if it adopted this conformation.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: An adjacent histidine (H53) in Mcl-1 would be expected to clash with R3c if it adopted the conformation seen in Bfl-1:FS2.
source: In Mcl-1, there is an alanine (A55) at this site, and an adjacent histidine (H53) would be expected to clash with R3c if it adopted this conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: The N-terminus of FS2 is buried further into the binding groove of Bfl-1 than Mcl-1.
source: The N-terminus of FS2 is also buried further into the binding groove of Bfl-1 than Mcl-1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The Bfl-1 binding groove is wider in the region between helices 3 and 4 than the Mcl-1 binding groove.
source: The Bfl-1 binding groove is wider in this region than the Mcl-1 binding groove, as illustrated by aligning many Bfl-1 and Mcl-1 structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is an amino acid insertion in the loop between helices 3 and 4 that is unique to Bfl-1.
source: There is an amino acid insertion in the loop between helices 3 and 4 that is unique to Bfl-1 that likely contributes to the distinct structural environment of Bfl-1 in this region (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment and structural analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amino acid insertion in the loop between helices 3 and 4 likely contributes to the distinct structural environment of Bfl-1 in this region.
source: There is an amino acid insertion in the loop between helices 3 and 4 that is unique to Bfl-1 that likely contributes to the distinct structural environment of Bfl-1 in this region (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: Designed peptides were tested for Bfl-1 selective targeting by carrying out BH3 profiling of cells with known dependencies on anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: We tested our designed peptides for Bfl-1 selective targeting by carrying out BH3 profiling of cells with known dependencies on anti-apoptotic proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: In the BH3 profiling assay, peptides are titrated into permeabilized cells, and mitochondrial depolarization is measured using the voltage-sensitive dye JC-1.
source: In this assay, peptides are titrated into permeabilized cells, and mitochondrial depolarization is measured using the voltage-sensitive dye JC-1 (Figure 7A) (Deng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the BH3 profiling assay, with a citation to Deng et al., 2007, and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: BCR-ABL-expressing B-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell lines engineered to depend on Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 or Bfl-1 overexpression for survival were tested.
source: We tested the apoptotic sensitivity of BCR-ABL-expressing B-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell lines engineered to depend on Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 or Bfl-1 overexpression for survival (Koss et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the cell lines used, with a citation to Koss et al., 2016.

claim: At 100 nM, the Bfl-1 selective inhibitors FS1, FS2 and FS3 promoted depolarization only in Bfl-1 dependent cells.
source: In comparison with a shorter, truncated PUMA BH3 (PUMA1e-4c, PUMAsh), which promoted mitochondrial depolarization in all of the cell lines tested, at 100 nM the Bfl-1 selective inhibitors FS1, FS2 and FS3 promoted depolarization only in Bfl-1 dependent cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays.

claim: Truncated PUMA BH3 (PUMA1e-4c, PUMAsh) promoted mitochondrial depolarization in all of the cell lines tested.
source: In comparison with a shorter, truncated PUMA BH3 (PUMA1e-4c, PUMAsh), which promoted mitochondrial depolarization in all of the cell lines tested, at 100 nM the Bfl-1 selective inhibitors FS1, FS2 and FS3 promoted depolarization only in Bfl-1 dependent cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays.

claim: An inactive PUMAsh mutant, PUMA L3aA;D3fA (PUMA 2A) was used as a negative control.
source: An inactive PUMAsh mutant, PUMA L3aA;D3fA (PUMA 2A) was used as a negative control (Ryan and Letai, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with a citation to Ryan and Letai, 2013.

claim: EC50 values for inducing mitochondrial permeabilization in the engineered cell lines agreed well with trends in Bfl-1-binding affinities.
source: EC50 values for inducing mitochondrial permeabilization in the engineered cell lines agreed well with trends in Bfl-1-binding affinities, as expected based on the mechanism of action (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cytochrome c release was measured in the same cell lines as an additional test for on-pathway activity.
source: As an additional test for on-pathway activity, we measured cytochrome c release in the same engineered cell lines in response to peptide treatment, using iBH3 profiling (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with a citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The specificity pattern observed when monitoring cytochrome c release was consistent with that obtained by BH3 profiling read out using JC-1.
source: The specificity pattern observed when monitoring cytochrome c release was consistent with that obtained by BH3 profiling read out using JC-1 (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the iBH3 profiling assays, shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A Mcl-1 selective peptide, MS1 was used as a control.
source: A Mcl-1 selective peptide, MS1 was used as a control (Foight et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with a citation to Foight et al., 2014.

claim: FS3 promoted mitochondrial depolarization more potently than FS1 or FS2.
source: In both assays, FS3 promoted mitochondrial depolarization more potently than FS1 or FS2, but was less selective, with significant cross reactivity at 30 μM peptide concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays.

claim: FS3 was less selective than FS1 or FS2, with significant cross reactivity at 30 μM peptide concentration.
source: In both assays, FS3 promoted mitochondrial depolarization more potently than FS1 or FS2, but was less selective, with significant cross reactivity at 30 μM peptide concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays.

claim: PUMA BH3 has been proposed to directly activate apoptosis through interactions with BAK and BAX.
source: FS1, FS2 and FS3 were based on the sequence of PUMA BH3, which has been proposed to directly activate apoptosis through interactions with BAK and BAX (Dai et al., 2014; Edwards et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dai et al., 2014 and Edwards et al., 2013.

claim: Cytochrome c release was measured in two 'unprimed' cell lines (PC-3 and SF295) to test whether FS1, FS2 or FS3 may directly activate BAK and BAX.
source: To test the possibility that FS1, FS2 or FS3 may directly activate BAK and BAX, we measured cytochrome c release in two 'unprimed' cell lines (PC-3 and SF295).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Unprimed cells require BAK/BAX activators to release cytochrome c.
source: Unprimed cells require BAK/BAX activators to release cytochrome c (Certo et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Certo et al., 2006.

claim: Cytochrome c release was observed in cells treated with BIM or PUMA BH3.
source: We observed cytochrome c release in cells treated with BIM or PUMA BH3 but not in cells treated with as much as 100 μM FS1 or FS2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the cytochrome c release assays, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cytochrome c release was not observed in cells treated with as much as 100 μM FS1 or FS2.
source: We observed cytochrome c release in cells treated with BIM or PUMA BH3 but not in cells treated with as much as 100 μM FS1 or FS2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the cytochrome c release assays, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with FS3 or PUMAsh peptide only led to cytochrome c release at high concentrations (~30-100 μM).
source: Treatment with FS3 or PUMAsh peptide only led to cytochrome c release at high concentrations (~30-100 μM) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the cytochrome c release assays, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: FS3 and PUMAsh may have very weak activator function.
source: This may indicate that FS3 and PUMAsh have very weak activator function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cytochrome c release data.

claim: FS1 and FS2 are not themselves activators.
source: Taken together, our data show that FS1 and FS2 are not themselves activators, but that they instead act as apoptotic sensitizers by competing with activators or with BAX or BAK for binding to anti-apoptotic proteins, as intended in our design scheme.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cytochrome c release data.

claim: FS1 and FS2 act as apoptotic sensitizers by competing with activators or with BAX or BAK for binding to anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: Taken together, our data show that FS1 and FS2 are not themselves activators, but that they instead act as apoptotic sensitizers by competing with activators or with BAX or BAK for binding to anti-apoptotic proteins, as intended in our design scheme.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cytochrome c release data.

claim: Initial sorts for Bfl-1 selective binders identified many sequences that included cysteine at position 1g or 2b.
source: Our initial sorts for Bfl-1 selective binders identified many sequences that included cysteine at position 1g or 2b (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the screening, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cysteines encoded at several other positions along the BH3 motif were not enriched.
source: Interestingly, cysteines encoded at several other positions along the BH3 motif were not enriched.
evidence: This is a finding from the screening.

claim: Cysteine was not enriched in previous screens for Bfl-1 binding.
source: Furthermore, cysteine was not enriched in previous screens for Bfl-1 binding (Dutta et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dutta et al., 2013.

claim: Bfl-1 binding selectivity could be improved in non-reducing conditions if the peptide ligand formed a disulfide bond with cysteine 55 (C55) of Bfl-1.
source: This observation led us to hypothesize that Bfl-1 binding selectivity could be improved in non-reducing conditions if the peptide ligand formed a disulfide bond with cysteine 55 (C55) of Bfl-1, which is adjacent to the binding cleft of Bfl-1 and unique to Bfl-1 among Bcl-2 family paralogs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the screening results, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Cysteine 55 (C55) of Bfl-1 is adjacent to the binding cleft of Bfl-1.
source: This observation led us to hypothesize that Bfl-1 binding selectivity could be improved in non-reducing conditions if the peptide ligand formed a disulfide bond with cysteine 55 (C55) of Bfl-1, which is adjacent to the binding cleft of Bfl-1 and unique to Bfl-1 among Bcl-2 family paralogs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Cysteine 55 (C55) is unique to Bfl-1 among Bcl-2 family paralogs.
source: This observation led us to hypothesize that Bfl-1 binding selectivity could be improved in non-reducing conditions if the peptide ligand formed a disulfide bond with cysteine 55 (C55) of Bfl-1, which is adjacent to the binding cleft of Bfl-1 and unique to Bfl-1 among Bcl-2 family paralogs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Testing yeast-displayed peptides for binding to a Bfl-1 cysteine-to-serine (C55S) mutant confirmed that PUMA and BIM bound to Bfl-1 C55S.

claim: The majority of the peptides in the cysteine-enriched pool bound to wild-type Bfl-1 but not to Bfl-1 C55S.
source: Testing yeast-displayed peptides for binding to a Bfl-1 cysteine-to-serine (C55S) mutant confirmed that PUMA and BIM bound to Bfl-1 C55S, whereas the majority of the peptides in the cysteine-enriched pool bound to wild-type Bfl-1 but not to Bfl-1 C55S (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the binding assays, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rescreening the library using Bfl-1 C55S led to the identification of FS1, FS2 and FS3.
source: Rescreening our library using Bfl-1 C55S led to the identification of FS1, FS2 and FS3, as described above.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The discovery that BH3 peptides in the library could access a unique, reactive cysteine in Bfl-1 led to the design of covalent inhibitors based on these peptides.
source: But, in addition, the discovery that BH3 peptides in our library could access a unique, reactive cysteine in Bfl-1 led us to design covalent inhibitors based on these peptides.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

evidence: This is a finding from the gel-shift assays, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Bfl-1 C55S contains two other solvent-exposed cysteine residues.
source: Both FS2_1gX and FS2_1fX modified Bfl-1 once or less when applied at micromolar concentrations, whereas Bfl-1 C55S (which contains two other solvent-exposed cysteine residues) did not react with these electrophilic peptides for at least 6 hr (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).

claim: FS2_1fX reacted with Bfl-1 with a half-life of 6.5 min.

claim: FS2_1fX was selective for Bfl-1 in BH3 profiling.
source: We tested FS2_1fX in BH3 profiling and found that it improved on-pathway targeting of Bfl-1 compared to N-terminally acetylated control (Figure 8E) and was selective for Bfl-1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the BH3 profiling assays, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: A crystal structure of FS2_1fX bound to Bfl-1 showed clear electron density consistent with a covalent bond to C55.
source: We solved a crystal structure of FS2_1fX bound to Bfl-1 that showed clear electron density consistent with a covalent bond to C55, as designed (Figure 8F,G).

claim: Selective targeting agents will likely be critical for disentangling the roles of different anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: Because the role of Bfl-1 in disease is less characterized than that of Mcl-1 or Bcl-2, selective targeting agents will likely be critical for disentangling the roles of different anti-apoptotic proteins.

source: Prior efforts to identify Bfl-1 selective inhibitors provided molecules with only modest binding affinity and/or selectivity (Mathieu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2012; Cashman et al., 2010; Zhai et al., 2008; Dutta et al., 2013).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Letai et al., 2002.
